land_owner.value: The ground was entered by Robert A Kenzie, 7 May 1831
land_owner.note: KINZIE'S ADDITION. The north fraction of section 10 is the section north of the river, which is why the register prints 102.29 acres and not a quarter's 160. It is resolved as the section's own grid box clipped to the committed north bank of the main stem (`e1834_harbor_cut/shoreline.geojson`), so no boundary here is authored. The two rows the register carries for it — one plain, one with the school-section marker — are the same entry printed twice. THE REGISTER SPELLS THE PURCHASER MORE THAN ONE WAY for this same tract — Robert A Kenzie; Robert A Kinzie — and the spellings are carried rather than merged, which is the land_sales crosswalk's standing rule: tract agreement is where two spellings MIGHT be one man and is never proof that they are. THE ROOF IS AN INVENTION AND THIS CANNOT OUTRANK IT. The footprint stands 52 m inside the tract's nearest boundary, which on a documented building would carry the middle tier, but this building was dealt to its lot by a recipe and is not there. The tract is real and the register's words about it are read; what is graded here is the claim that THIS roof stands on it, and that claim is the recipe's. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

persons.name: Stephen M. Salisbury
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'Stephen M. Salesbuc' and 'Stephen M. Salisbury' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the Democrat of 26 November 1833, column 31; the Democrat of 3 December 1833, column 7. The corpus associates the name with the Dupage; that is where the paper does business with this person and not a statement about where they slept, and the storefront tickets are the ones that may stand a shop there. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `justice_of_the_peace` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry.

Every other record in this dataset argues for a household — a family the sources count, or a trade the town demonstrably needed. This one argues for a PERSON: the Democrat and the American name Stephen M. Salisbury as a justice of the peace at Chicago 2 time(s), and this reconstruction did not hold them. `data/residents/` has no way to carry a person except inside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing: one member, no dwelling, no division, no origin, no arrival beyond the bound the paper sets. Reading a family, a house or a quarter of town into this record would be reading something the papers do not say. tools/mint_documented_residents.py derives the whole minted set and prints every candidate it refused, with the reason.

persons.name: Samuel Shaw
persons.note: PROJECTED RESIDENT. Documented in Chicago post-office evidence but not independently corroborated strongly enough for attested circa-1835 residence. KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Samuel Shaw: » ;' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 1 April 1834, column 2 — dated 1834-04-01. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1). THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Shaw, Mrs. Sarah J. | Profession. | March 6, 1867.” (second_presb_0304, printed page 171), admitted 1867-03-06 by profession. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Shaw' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins S. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a_married_womans_entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

persons.name: Charles C. Williams
persons.note: GRADED BY THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER — rule G2e, applied 2026-09-04. This identity is inferred because that rung fired on the civic and press rows recorded on this card, which the resident-research corpus does not read. This programme's letter-list rule of 2026-09-02 would call it a projected resident on the absence of a research row; it is superseded here, and a no-find in one corpus is not a finding about another (T-0822). KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Williams, Charles C.' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 22 October 1834, column 7 — dated 1834-10-22. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1). THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Williams, Mrs. Carrie C. | Letter. | March 2, 1870.” (second_presb_0368, printed page 174), admitted 1870-03-02 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Williams' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins C. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a_married_womans_entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.
